transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-23
Start: 10:00 AM PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Quantaco Head of ML), Ethan Ross (Quantaco SRE), Jonas Mueller (Quantaco Product), Sara Li (Quantaco Finance)

[00:00] Alex Rivera: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have about 45 minutes; main agenda is cost econ, caching and batching follow-ups from last week. quick check — are there any new items?

[00:18] Priya Kapoor: no new items from my side, just want to dig into the tokens per dollar numbers — sara's on because finance wants clear tradeoffs.

[00:30] Maya Chen: cool, i'll kick off with the latest bench numbers we ran on the 13B variant with awq-int8 and fp16 for baseline. note, some of the numbers are noisy since the seq distribution in the test harness wasn't perfectly matched to quantaco's production traces.

[00:45] Maya Chen: so summary — awq-int8 gave us ~2.6x improvement in tokens/sec per GPU vs fp16 but latency p95 increased by ~10 to 15 ms on longer contexts, and memory footprint dropped which allowed larger batch sizes. caching (prefix + kv) gave us another 1.3x improvement on hits, but depends heavily on hit rate. our measured token/sec/$ metric assumes on-demand hosted pricing; dedicated pricing improves unit cost but has commit tradeoffs.

[01:12] Ethan Ross: quick q — when you say tokens/sec/$ is that including infra overhead and rate limiting? sara and i want the number we can present to finance, like fully loaded unit cost.

[01:25] Alex Rivera: good question. the spreadsheet I sent was a host-model view: it included GPU amortization and the Redwood hosted baseline. it didn't include ingress/egress networking or SRE staffing. we can produce a fully loaded view — that's on my next steps.

[01:40] Jonas Mueller: also curious — how does batching affect real latency for the user? our product needs low single-request latency for chat plus throughput for async scoring.

[01:52] Liam O'Neill: yeah, batching is a tradeoff. at small QPS (sub-50 rps) batching aggressively increases latency; at high QPS you get better tokens/sec/$ with minimal p95 change. for chat we recommend adaptive batching with a strict latency cap and a short max batch delay (e.g., 10ms). for scoring workloads you can increase batch windows.

[02:20] Priya Kapoor: can you walk through a concrete example — say 512-token average seq, 1000 QPS with 40% cache hit? what's tokens/sec/$ hosted vs dedicated?

[02:32] Maya Chen: sure — off the cuff: in our hosted baseline with fp16, at 512 tokens avg and no caching, you might see ~120k tokens/sec per GPU and a unit cost of X (we'll share numbers in spreadsheet). with awq-int8 and 40% prefix hits you'd move effectively to ~200k tokens/sec equivalent and unit cost drops ~35%. on dedicated, because you amortize reserved capacity, token $ can drop another ~20% but you need to commit and handle peak bursts. i'll put exact numbers in the updated model.

[03:05] Sara Li: finance needs the assumptions up front — what's cache hit rate sensitivity, and we need a best/worst case. also need to see the cost of incorrect cache invalidation or low hit periods.

[03:20] Maya Chen: totally — we'll include sensitivity curves. in our experiments cache hit rate sensitivity is significant: going from 40% to 20% can double effective cost per served token for some conversational flows that have small reusable prefixes. but for template-driven scoring where prefixes are long, caches are extremely effective.

[03:45] Ethan Ross: on the SRE side, i'd like to see how KV cache replication and warm-up behavior look for dedicated vs hosted — i.e., when you spin up a new pod or a failover, what's the cold-cache penalty?

[03:58] Liam O'Neill: good callout. cold-starts are real — our runtime keeps an LRU of recent prefixes but if you see a spike and traffic is routed to a different node, initial misses will add latency and cost. for high-availability dedicated setups we recommend cross-node pre-warming for critical prefixes and sticky routing for sessions. we'll document expected warm-up curves.

[04:30] Priya Kapoor: any notes on sequence length distribution? our prod has a bimodal distribution — quick chat messages ~40 tokens and long policy docs ~2k tokens. how do we model that?

[04:45] Maya Chen: we need the histogram — ethan said he'd send it. but generally, batching helps high seq lengths because you amortize KV cache management and attention compute. however, long sequences increase KV cache memory usage and can reduce batch sizes. quantization tends to help memory so it indirectly enables larger batches for long seqs.

[05:08] Alex Rivera: ok, let's talk about the experiments we agreed to run this week and the timeline. Maya?

[05:15] Maya Chen: i'll run a focused throughput test with awq-int8 at target 4k tokens/sec sustained for 10 minutes using your sample traces — that'll show stable tokens/sec and p95 behavior. i'll also run a sensitivity run for cache hit rates at 20/40/60%. i'll aim to post results by Fri 7/30.

[05:38] Ethan Ross: i'll send the seq length histogram and QPS patterns by end of day Tue 7/25. also note any compliance or network/firewall needs for dedicated pilot — we have a ticketing process.

[05:50] Priya Kapoor: from product — we want the latency SLOs mapped to user tiers. e.g., premium chat 200ms p95, standard chat 400ms p95, batch scoring can be >2s. can Redwood's routing enforce per-route latency policies?

[06:07] Liam O'Neill: yes — smart routing can route by latency SLOs and fall back to cheaper model variants if SLO would be violated. but with quantization you sometimes see a slight quality delta; we suggest running eval prompts to detect regression for critical flows.

[06:30] Jonas Mueller: what's the plan for quality checks? we can't sacrifice user experience for cost.

[06:36] Maya Chen: we recommend a small eval set tied to functional tests — we'll run the eval across fp16 and awq-int8 and share regression metrics (ROUGE/EM/LL?) and a handful of human-reviewed samples. the Redwood Optimize tooling can alert on per-prompt regression.

[06:58] Sara Li: on pricing — please include a hosted vs dedicated 12-month comparison with break-even point. finance will use that to decide commit size.

[07:10] Alex Rivera: will do. i'll model commit tiers and burst capacity costs. also include optional add-ons like longer observability retention and premium SLA.

[07:25] Priya Kapoor: one more technical: when you mention batching windows and max-delay, is that tunable per route?

[07:33] Liam O'Neill: yes per-route batching policy is available; you can set max-latency, max-batch-size, and prioritization. for chat we recommend max-delay 5-15ms, for scoring 50-100ms. we'll provide recommended defaults.

[07:50] Maya Chen: small note — the current test harness sometimes reports speaker misalignment; ignore a few odd transcribed names, the metrics are valid.

[08:00] Alex Rivera: recap then next steps: maya runs the awq-int8 throughput + cache sensitivity by 7/30; ethan shares traffic profile by 7/25; alex circulates updated cost model by 7/26; priya confirms internal stakeholders by 7/28. we'll schedule a dedicated benchmark next Wed 7/30 — tentative.

[08:20] Priya Kapoor: sounds good. can sara and i get the spreadsheet with clear assumptions?

[08:27] Alex Rivera: yes i'll include assumptions and a best/worst case scenario.

[08:33] Jonas Mueller: any blockers?

[08:36] Ethan Ross: firewall ticket is a process but manageable — won't block the hosted benchmarking. for dedicated we'll need a security review.

[08:45] Priya Kapoor: ok thanks team. thanks redwood for the clear next steps.

[08:50] Alex Rivera: thanks all. we'll follow up in slack and send the updated artifacts. meeting adjourned.

[09:00] (call ends)
